newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FOCUS-Brazil urged to move cautiously on trade gap.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Brazil urged to move cautiously on trade gap.

text.p: Brazilian economists welcomed the government's announcement of modest plans to contain the nation's worsening trade deficit, saying the gap was not large enough to warrant drastic policy changes.

"The government should not take any hasty measures to stop this, like tinkering with foreign exchange policy, because it is a long-term structural problem," said Marcelo Allain, chief economist at BMC bank in Brazil.
"But it can do other things to stimulate exports, such as expanding credit and lowering port fees and electricty costs for businesses," Allain added.

Following a week of gloomy trade numbers that hurt Brazilian stocks and bonds in domestic and international markets, the government said Thursday it was mulling a list of possibilities to narrow the trade gap. They include:
* cutting interest charged on a $1.0 billion credit line for exporters from a current rate of about 20 percent a year
* raising the limit on the value of each loan available under the credit line
* lengthening the maturity period to 12 years from eight years on government loans to capital goods exporters
* offering new short-term credit to exporters of autoparts, fruit and furniture

Talk of the new measures follows last week's release of a much-larger-than expected September trade gap of $655 million and news that October's third week saw one of the lowest export volumes this year.

The numbers have led to speculation that the trade gap could rise above $1 billion in October. The government says the gap should not exceed $500 million, noting Septmeber's hike was due mostly to larger-than-expected oil imports.
The government has also put some of the blame for the gap on seasonal factors, such as declining soy exports and rising imports of consumer goods ahead of the Christmas season.

But economists note that on an annual level, import growth is simply outpacing that of exports and the economy. So far this year, imports have grown at an annual rate of about 10 percent compared to economic growth of about 2.5 percent and export growth of 5 percent, economists said.
Still, few think the widening trade gap, a trend which is expected to continue next year, should trigger alarm bells.

"The trade numbers through February will continue to look bad, but the possibility of financing the deficit looks good," said an economist at a leading U.S. bank who asked not to be named. "Foreign direct investment is surging and it will surge next year especially with privatizations," he added.
A Reuter survey this week of eight Brazilian brokerages and research firms forecasts a 1996 trade gap of $3.5 billion and an October trade gap of $723 million.
